toc.title: Why give an uncomfortable emotion permission?
Give your emotion an image and a welcome
If it's too much, start smaller

blocks.p: One of the things that may be keeping you stuck in an uncomfortable emotion is that you're not giving it permission to exist. You may be repressing it in some way, which is understandable. But that coping tactic can only last so long, and it might actually be making things worse.

Giving permission is the third of my three top-down self-regulation openers. It comes after validation and normalization. I'll briefly review those two, and then teach you how to give yourself permission to have your emotion, or your emotions.

Giving permission simply means you're allowing your emotion to be with you in the present moment. You don't minimize, deny, excuse, or ignore it, or use any other sort of reflexive cognitive adaptation to reduce its intensity. You are absolutely not the only person to cope this way. It's very common, probably something we all do on some level.

It's possible to shift your emotional state from the bottom up or from the top down: from the body to the brain, or from the brain to the body, with the brainstem acting as the intermediary. Top-down self-regulation openers can help with that. Mine are validation, normalization, and giving permission. They lay the groundwork for further techniques you can use, and they also help to soften the intensity of the negative emotions you're experiencing.
Ever so briefly:

ul: Validation is recognizing the factual matter that your emotions exist. It doesn't mean you're okay with it or that you like it. It just means you recognize the emotion is real. Validation is kind of like confirming.

Normalization is making sense of your now valid emotions based on the context they exist in or came from. That could be the immediate context, the past context of your life and how it affects you in the present moment, or both.

blocks.h: Why give an uncomfortable emotion permission?

blocks.p: Why would you give your emotions permission to exist? They're not comfortable, right? I know it might sound odd. But look at it this way: the emotion that needs permission to exist already exists within you anyway. It's already there, whether you like it or not, and whether you want it there or not. You've just successfully ignored, minimized, denied, stuffed down, neglected, or coped with it until this point. So now it might be time to do something different.

I'll ask you: isn't it exhausting to keep running away from or subduing the emotion that brings you here? Doesn't it leave you worn out, frustrated, or defeated? So instead of going down that road again, let's try a different one, if you can handle it: just giving the emotion permission to exist. When you allow the emotion to be present, it can actually further reduce its intensity.
Dr. Porges described what changes when you stop holding your body's feelings down:

q: When you feel your body, you no longer are using all your... neural energy to suppress bodily feelings.
blocks.cite: Stephen Porges, [From Sound to Safety: Understanding the Safe & Sound Protocol with Dr. Porges and Karen Onderko (episode 254)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/20b541da-11ef-4b2e-b911-42b6ceba2bd1)

blocks.p: Instead of those reflexive cognitive coping skills, and instead of a behavioral adaptation, your challenge on this step of your journey might be to just allow the emotion to be present. Here's what that might sound like:

ul: "I'm allowed to have the emotion of..." and then fill in the blank.
"I'm allowed to feel what I have inside."
"Other people are allowed to have emotions, and I'm allowed to also."
"I feel them whether I want to or not. I might as well give myself permission."
"I'm going to allow myself to feel and be curious about the emotional experience of my traumatized state," or of my defensive state, or just of this current moment.

blocks.p: Pick one that feels right for you, or make up your own. What would it sound like to give yourself permission to have the emotion you do have?
You can connect all three top-down self-regulation openers:

ol: Validate. Ask yourself, "Is my emotion valid?" Does it actually exist?
Normalize. If yes, ask, "Is my emotion normal?" Does it make sense that I'm experiencing this, based on my life context?
Give permission. If yes to both, allow it. Give it permission to be there.

blocks.h: Give your emotion an image and a welcome

blocks.p: There's one more technique for giving permission, and it might be more inviting: create an image and a welcoming message for your emotion. This is something I recommend to my clients. It's a playful, metaphorical, cognitive technique to make the process of allowing your emotion more manageable. As you keep practicing, eventually you won't need it.

It might sound like this: "You're welcome to be here with me, sadness. You're welcome to be here with me, anger. I'm going to stick you in my pocket and let you hang out with me." And then you imagine tucking it away into your pocket.

I know it's silly. That's the point. The point of the image is to have fun with it. The point of this image, or any of this, is not to ignore your emotion. Tucking it into your pocket is not meant to be ignoring. If that feels dismissive to you, create another one, whatever image helps you feel like you're allowing the emotion to be present with you. Maybe the emotion is walking beside you throughout your day, or sitting on your shoulder. It really doesn't matter. It's just an image, a metaphor. If you have one that allows the emotion to be with you in compassion, run with that.

Speaking of compassion, make sure you anchor in safety to allow your emotion to be with you. When you're anchored in your safety state, your curiosity about your stuck defensive state emotions will probably be higher. Your tolerance for allowing them to be present will probably be higher too.

If you're not in your safety state enough, then you probably shouldn't be doing this, in my opinion. If you try to allow the emotion to be present and you're not ready for it, it may trigger some dysregulation. If that happens, you're just not ready for this yet, and that's okay.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: If it's too much, start smaller

blocks.p: Maybe giving permission is too much for you, even with the silly image, and even when you're anchored in your safety state. That's fine. There are other places to start.

Start with a recent, tolerable emotion. Not something that stems directly from your childhood or the thing you went through. Just a recent one, maybe something you felt earlier in the day. These might be emotions like irritability, worry or concern, mild sadness, or disinterest. As best you can, come from compassion, curiosity, and your safety state. Then:

ol: Normalize it based on the context.
Allow it to be present, with a silly image and a message for it.

blocks.p: Or start with a positive emotion. I don't actually believe emotions are negative. Defensive state emotions aren't good or bad, negative or positive. But just as a framework: if defensive state emotions are too much for you, you can practice this process with a more positive emotion, and think of it as practice. Calm or relaxation, happiness, joy, or connection. Start with those. Maybe those are things you can allow and give permission to be present.

Further down your trauma recovery journey, after allowing the emotion to exist, you'll also give the defensive polyvagal state that underlies your emotion permission to complete the impulse connected to it.

Here we're just working on the emotion. But underneath it are sensations, and the impulse of the polyvagal state. There's a good chance you're stuck in a defensive state, and that you went through something that didn't allow your impulse to survive to complete. Even if you didn't, no matter where you are on your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system), there's going to be some impulse to climb up the ladder. Eventually that's a process you need to allow to happen and to complete. Validating, normalizing, and giving permission help to open up the potential for that self-regulation process to happen.

I gave you three, but there's actually one more top-down self-regulation opener. Since your emotions are valid, they're normal, and they have permission to exist, what if you affirmed that you are worth it, and that you are worth the effort it takes to get unstuck? That fourth one is affirmation.
